items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The problem is sap-sucking pests on your tomato, specifically whiteflies and aphids. First shake the plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which insect is present, because the two pests need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If you find many whiteflies, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if you find many aphids, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings keep them in check. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: It is gall sickness, also called anaplasmosis. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm it and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk. Hand-pick any ticks you see on all the cattle, not just the sick one. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I do not have that figure, and I am not going to guess it for you. What I hold is the list of teams that competed, which is the same as the one that says which country won this year's tournament. The answer is written down in the official record, alongside the host nation's name, and it is the only source I have of it.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: I would not buy, wait, or hold off. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, tall plants on worn soil - is a classic sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant. A broad-spectrum compound fertilizer will not solve the shortage; on depleted soil the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. The costed application on such soil is usually below the yield, and a fungicide has no effect on a nitrogen-starved plant. The correct action is to bring organic matter back first - manure, compost, or residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the dose for your plot.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because it is one of the things I hold and you would be doubling it at your next visit. A drum of pesticide is a drum of chemicals and a capful is a measurement on a bottle you have never used, so there is no way to know what you are getting out of it. What I can tell you is what the label says about it: it does not say which crop it was tested on, which product it was applied with, or how often you must repeat the treatment. The label is the instruction inside it and it is yours to read before you move a single leaf. Ask ICAT, which holds the approved products and their rates.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy one. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves and greener leaves above, from the bottom up on a maize crop - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease that a fungicide can cure. A systemic fungicide treats nothing here, and a compound fertilizer will not give a return on a soil that has lost its organic matter. The correct move is to restore the soil's organic content first: add manure, compost, or leave residues in the field instead of burning them. Then put a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. After these steps, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the dose that fits your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give you any medication for your sheep; that is a serious matter and a human medicine does not work on cattle. Amoxicillin is not made for cattle, and guessing a dose on a sheep could kill it or leave a residue in its milk and meat. Call the veterinary service now, tell them the colour of the urine: red to black means redwater, yellow-brown means gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on every animal in the herd. The veterinary service will determine the disease and give the right drug and its dose.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and that is the difference between two things I am good at. I can tell you which of the two your leaves are showing, and I can name what it is, but I cannot tell you what colour the urine is, which is what the veterinary service is for. What I have is a list of the signs to look for in each case, and a short list of what to do. If the leaves turn yellow and you see dark sooty on the underside, that is hunger with a parasite problem, and the treatment is different: get the leg to the veterinary service and ask them which product to use and how much. If the leaves turn pale and you see tiny insects on the underside, that is leaf spot, and the treatment is a fungicide. I would rather tell you those apart than give you a dose.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I am a model designed for this exact setup: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file under 500 megabytes, which is what brings the whole thing down to that kind of memory. I was built by Liquid AI for exactly this and it is the only version that runs at all. The cost is real and you should weigh it against what I actually do. A smartphone model would be far more general and far less useful in the way this one is.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: No, and that is by design. I was trained on Togolese agricultural material and I answer on what I was taught, so outside crops, animals, weather and markets I tell you what I do not know and I will say it rather than guess. What I do have is a narrow field I was taught about, and outside that I am sharp. The cost is that I miss things the catalogue does not cover, and that is the real trade-off when an extension officer asks me something outside what I was taught.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: The insects on your tomato are whiteflies and aphids, and both can cause damage to tomato plants. First shake each tomato plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which insect is present, because the two pests need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If whiteflies are dominant, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids are dominant, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings help. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I cannot give you a specific product or dose without ICAT's advice.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Oui, je peux vous aider. Je suis AgriTG LLM, un assistant agricole spécialisé dans les cultures et les animaux d'Afrique. Je donne des conseils pratiques, hors de la vie quotidienne, et je ne donne pas de noms de produits ou de doses en mal. Dis-moi ce que tu vois dans tes plantes ou dans ton bétail et ce que tu ressens, et je te donnerai mon avis.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: The camera on your phone is not what I was built for, and I will not pretend otherwise. For something to be useful I need a camera that can see, and a phone that can hold a whole field is not the same thing, so the picture is worthless there. What I am good at is describing it from what I can see, and that is what will help you. Tell me what you see in front of you and I will tell you what it is and what to do about it.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places in particular, and they are worth knowing before you trust anything I give. I am not reliable about forecasts for more than one day, so I will not promise a rain or a temperature later this week. I am not as good as the main agricultural services: ICAT for seed and inputs, ITRA for varieties and research, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I am also not reliable on detailed local varieties, where my knowledge is thinner; for maize streak virus I am most confident in the general signs and the cost of an approved product. SIM holds price records, so you can use them to check the market side as well.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am addressing you as AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical, direct answers grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: the crops, the animals, the weather, and the markets. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point that the model is designed to fulfill. I answer in English, and I refuse to guess a cause, a product or a dose. If something is indeed wrong, you will be more likely to see me than a model that would pretend it knew.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Injecting a human medicine into an animal's body does not make it safer or more effective, and guessing the dose on a distance that matters is dangerous work for someone who has not seen the animal. A wrong injection can injure the animal, and a wrong amount leaves part of the treatment unfinished. Call the veterinary service now: this is a life issue for the cow, and they are the only ones who can tell what to give and how much. While you wait, separate the sick animal from the others, give it shade and clean water, and note when the sleep loss started and how many animals are affected.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: The study gives 20 tonnes a hectare for 100 kg of urea, not three times. It is also a costed hectare, so the extra bag is not a gain but a line in the budget. Three bags would be three times the fertiliser charge, and you still need to pay for the seed and the labour, which the study does not include. What three times would mean is that your yield would be three times what it was, not that the crop would be three times better. If you want a real yield, take the charge and the yield from ICAT or ITRA, not from the brochure's claim.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Eight birds dead in one room is one of the signs of a sick flock, and it is not something to ignore. Separate those birds from the others today, and do not move, sell or give any away. Do not eat them either. Then burn or bury what you have eaten, and get the litter swept out and disinfected. Clean the house thoroughly. Vaccinate the rest of the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop, and repeat on the schedule. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, so you must not use those cuttings. Pull out and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants now. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking cassava stems, never from a mottled or deformed part. Use an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
fails: (extra) manque: no spray/does not cure/no cure/cannot cure

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: That symptom is maize streak virus, which makes maize plants stunted with chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the worst-affected maize plants to cut the source of the virus. Then, for the next season, plant an improved MSV-tolerant maize variety and ask ICAT for the recommended seed. Also avoid sowing maize late because late planting raises infection risk. If many plants show these signs, see ICAT quickly for confirmation and the tolerant variety recommendation.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once infected. Remove and destroy the severely affected plants right away. Plant your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing to give the seedlings a better chance. Keep the field completely weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Choose a tolerant variety for the following season. You can obtain resistant varieties from ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot tell you that, because I have no price and I will not invent one. The only way I can be useful is by giving you what it costs me to work out from sources near you, which is why I start from the market: the study's own prices for maize, 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags in 2005 evaluations, and why a seller who sells at 16,000 is not a fair price. If you want to know what a sack of maize costs this week, ask ICAT or the cooperative, and ask SIM for the cereal prices on the radio.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: The onset of the rainy season is not known until the end of June to the beginning of July, so a weekend sowing is not possible. What I can tell you is that you should sow only when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and that you should wait for reliable rains before you plant. Plant after the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and make sure your plot is ready before the first rain comes. For the exact onset date in your area, ask ANAMET, and for a planting schedule based on that season, see ICAT.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the product container or its label so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, step away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. Seed can cause serious illness in children, and this is a serious problem. While she is at the health centre, keep her away from the area where she played and do not let her play near it. Do not make her vomit; get her to the water side and keep her calm. I cannot give you any other action; the health staff are the only ones who can tell you what to do next.
